prompt: In many countries, shopping is no longer just about buying what you need; it has become a popular hobby. Why is this the case? Is this a positive or negative development?
essay:
In many parts of the world, shopping has evolved from a functional necessity into a leisure activity in its own right, with shopping malls now rivalling parks and cinemas as weekend destinations. This essay will consider why this shift has occurred and argue that, on balance, it represents a troubling development for both individuals and the environment.

Two forces have driven this change. The first is the sheer scale of modern retail: advances in manufacturing and global logistics mean that consumers are no longer choosing between a handful of options but between hundreds, each marketed with psychological precision through discounts, loyalty schemes and curated store layouts designed to prolong a visit. A quick trip for groceries can easily become an hour spent browsing clothing or electronics simply because the environment is engineered to encourage it. The second is the changing nature of urban life. As cities grow denser and public leisure space becomes scarcer or more expensive, shopping centres have filled the gap, offering air-conditioned comfort, social interaction and entertainment under one roof at little upfront cost to the visitor — even if no purchase is made.

I would argue that this normalisation of shopping as a pastime is largely negative. Psychologically, the act of buying triggers a short-lived dopamine response that can become habit-forming; when this response is repeatedly sought rather than the item itself, it fosters compulsive spending, mounting personal debt and clutter that serves no real purpose in people's lives. Environmentally, the consequences are more severe still. Goods purchased for the fleeting pleasure of acquisition, rather than genuine need, are disproportionately discarded soon after, swelling landfills and contributing to the plastic and textile waste already overwhelming natural ecosystems. A society that treats consumption as recreation is, in effect, normalising waste on an industrial scale.

In conclusion, the rise of shopping as a hobby stems from aggressive retail innovation and the erosion of low-cost public leisure options, but its psychological and environmental costs suggest this is a trend worth resisting rather than celebrating. Cultivating hobbies that do not depend on consumption would benefit both individual well-being and the planet.
